content: The prevalence of HIV infection among children with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) was significant, with 45% of children in the confirmed MDR-TB group and 15% in the unconfirmed group being HIV-positive. HIV testing was relatively comprehensive. A large proportion of children exhibited chest radiographic or extrapulmonary disease features consistent with severe tuberculosis (TB), as well as malnutrition, as outlined in the 2016 WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant TB. Despite these challenges, overall treatment outcomes were favorable, even in the context of HIV co-infection and severe disease, demonstrating that good outcomes are achievable in children with MDR-TB. The analysis of individual second-line drugs revealed several important findings. Among children with confirmed MDR-TB, only 1% of studies reported safety outcomes. However, children with clinically diagnosed (unconfirmed) MDR-TB, who generally had less severe disease, achieved good outcomes without the use of second-line injectable drugs. This supports the practice of using injectable-sparing regimens in children with less severe disease to avoid severe adverse events (SAEs) associated with second-line injectables, without compromising treatment outcomes. High-dose isoniazid was frequently used, particularly in South African sites, often in combination with ethionamide or prothionamide. Later-generation fluoroquinolones, primarily moxifloxacin, did not appear to provide a significant treatment benefit, although their limited use (in only 10% of cases) may have obscured potential advantages. These findings regarding individual drug effects should be interpreted within the context of multidrug regimens used for MDR-TB treatment. The quality of the included studies was generally low, as most were retrospective or prospective observational cohort studies, with no randomized controlled trials available for inclusion. Data on novel drugs such as delamanid and bedaquiline were not yet available for analysis. Additionally, the sample size of children with confirmed extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) was very small. Toxicity was often poorly assessed, and missing data on HIV status were addressed through imputation. Missing data on nutritional status and disease severity were managed using a composite disease severity variable. In summary, this pediatric-specific individual patient data (IPD) analysis has provided valuable information for the development of clinically and programmatically relevant treatment guidelines. The proportion of children achieving favorable treatment outcomes, even with severe TB and HIV co-infection, was encouraging. However, there is an urgent need for data on the use of novel drugs like bedaquiline and delamanid in children. Future research should focus on shorter treatment regimens (less than 18 months) and injectable-sparing regimens for children.
